hops.afterHeading: The glial ladder: from an inference to a movie
hops.title: Adult canaries keep their radial glia
hops.text: Adult canaries never take the glial ladder down. In 1987 Arturo Alvarez-Buylla and colleagues stained adult canary brains for vimentin and found radial glia reaching from the ventricle into the forebrain. The antibody marked radial glia in developing rats but none in adult rodents examined; the authors wondered whether adult neuron production explained the difference. The team later labelled newborn cells in adult birds and checked where they appeared. Some reached 5 millimetres from the ventricle; the fastest estimated rate, 28 micrometres an hour, was where radial glia were dense. Many neurons added to a male canary's song-control region in autumn, when it revises its song repertoire, survive eight months.

sources.citation: Alvarez-Buylla, Buskirk & Nottebohm, J. Comp. Neurol. 264:159-170 (1987)
Alvarez-Borda, Haripal & Nottebohm, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 101:3957-3961 (2004)

image.caption: Adult canaries keep radial glial fibres, and newborn neurons still migrate through their forebrain.

hops.afterHeading: The engine: what brings the nucleus up
hops.title: Blebbistatin and the blue-light problem
hops.text: Blebbistatin, found in 2003, blocks nonmuscle myosin II and stops a dividing cell's cleavage furrow from contracting. In 2004 a cell biologist tested it under common fluorescence excitation colours. Blue light at 450 to 490 nanometres killed cells that held the drug and also wrecked the drug, so it stopped blocking myosin. A 2005 study turned that into a trick: exposing cells to blue light switched the drug off and let a stalled furrow contract again, though irradiating blebbistatin may also generate damaging free radicals. In 2016 chemists reported para-aminoblebbistatin, which still blocks myosin II and held up under blue light with no detectable phototoxicity in the cells tested.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A fluorescence microscope shining blue light onto a glass dish beside amber bottles on a dim lab bench.
image.caption: Blue light used for fluorescence imaging can inactivate blebbistatin and, with the drug present, kill cells.

hops.title: A smooth brain is not the problem in lissencephaly
hops.text: Lissencephaly makes it tempting to think folds are what make a cortex work. A Florida manatee disagrees. Its brain, about the size of a grapefruit at roughly 360 grams, is the largest smooth brain in the animal kingdom, with a gyration index of 1.06; a separate study put six whale and dolphin species at about 5.4 on average. Yet Florida manatees find warm and fresh water and thread the maze of channels in the Ten Thousand Islands. Their nearly smooth cortex has organized layers, clearly defined in some regions. In classic human lissencephaly, the cortex is also abnormally thick and poorly layered, because many neurons stalled before reaching their places.

sources.citation: Cook, Bauer & Reep, Front. Behav. Neurosci. 19:1576378 (2025)
Reep et al., Brain Behav. Evol. 34:365-386 (1989)
Manger et al., J. Comp. Neurol. 520:2430-2439 (2012)
